items.title: Averaged Hermitian form for a compact group
items.statement: Assume AC. For a compact Hausdorff group K, a continuous finite-dimensional complex representation ρ:K→GL(V), and a Hermitian inner product h0 linear in the first variable, define h(v,w)=∫K h0(ρ(k)v,ρ(k)w) dμ(k), where μ is normalized Haar probability.

references.title: Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6
Vera Serganova, Representation Theory, Chapter III §§1.6–2.1

items.axiom_audit: AC is consumed only to obtain normalized Haar probability.
items.strategy: The integrand is continuous on compact K and scalar integrable. The normalized Haar probability is unique under AC; linearity in v, conjugate linearity in w, and Hermitian symmetry pass through scalar integration. Positive definiteness and invariance are established by the next lemma.

items.title: Invariant orthogonal complements in unitary representations
items.statement: For any strongly continuous unitary representation π of a topological group G on a complex Hilbert space H and any closed invariant subspace M, the orthogonal complement M⊥ is closed and invariant. This assertion is choice free.

references.title: Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6
Vera Serganova, Representation Theory, Chapter III §§1.6–2.1

items.axiom_audit: No choice principle enters the orthogonality calculation.
items.proof_strategy: For x∈M⊥, y∈M and g∈G, ⟨π(g)x,y⟩=⟨x,π(g−1)y⟩=0 because π(g−1)M=M. Thus π(g)M⊥⊆M⊥, and g−1 gives equality. M⊥ is the intersection of kernels of the continuous functionals x↦⟨x,y⟩, so it is closed.

items.title: Averaging unitarizes a finite-dimensional compact-group representation
items.statement: Assume AC. The averaged form of a continuous finite-dimensional complex representation of a compact Hausdorff group is a positive-definite K-invariant Hermitian form, so the representation is unitary for that form.

references.title: Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6
Vera Serganova, Representation Theory, Chapter III §§1.6–2.1

items.axiom_audit: AC supplies the normalized Haar measure; the rest is finite-dimensional and scalar.
items.proof_strategy: For v≠0, k↦h0(ρ(k)v,ρ(k)v) is continuous, nonnegative and positive at e; it is bounded below on a nonempty open neighborhood, whose Haar mass is positive. Therefore h(v,v)>0. The change of variables k↦kg, licensed by right invariance of normalized Haar, gives h(ρ(g)v,ρ(g)w)=h(v,w). Finite-dimensional equivalent norms retain continuity.

items.title: Complete reducibility of finite-dimensional compact-group representations
items.statement: Assume AC. Every continuous finite-dimensional complex representation of a compact Hausdorff group is a finite direct sum of irreducible invariant subspaces.

references.title: Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6
Vera Serganova, Representation Theory, Chapter III §§1.6–2.1
David Vogan, Review of Harmonic Analysis on Compact Groups, §§2.1–2.16

items.axiom_audit: AC is used only through the Haar unitarization lemma.
items.proof_strategy: Unitarize by the preceding lemma. Induct on dim V: a nonzero representation either is irreducible or has a nonzero proper invariant subspace M. It is closed in finite dimension; its invariant orthogonal complement M⊥ gives V=M⊕M⊥, both of smaller dimension. Apply the finite induction hypothesis separately and concatenate the irreducible summands; the zero representation is the empty sum.

items.title: Haar averaging of bounded operators as a weak operator integral
items.statement: Assume AC. For strongly continuous unitary representations π on H and σ on J of compact Hausdorff K and any bounded T:H→J, define A(T) by ⟨A(T)v,w⟩=∫K⟨σ(k)Tπ(k)−1v,w⟩dμ(k). The displayed integral is a weak operator integral; no operator-norm continuity of the orbit of arbitrary T is assumed.

references.title: David Vogan, Review of Harmonic Analysis on Compact Groups, §§2.1–2.16
Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6

items.axiom_audit: AC supplies Haar probability and the Countable Choice hypothesis of Hilbert Riesz representation.
items.strategy: For fixed v,w the scalar integrand is continuous and bounded by ||T||||v||||w||. For fixed v, conjugate the integral to a bounded linear functional of w and apply Hilbert Riesz representation, then conjugate back; uniqueness gives A(T)v, linearity in v, and ||A(T)||≤||T||. The following lemma proves the full projection property and establishes the construction.

items.title: Haar averaging projects contractively onto bounded intertwiners
items.statement: Assume AC. For strongly continuous unitary π,σ of compact Hausdorff K, weak Haar averaging A:B(H,J)→B(H,J) is an idempotent contraction with range exactly Hom_K(H,J). Its operator norm is one when Hom_K(H,J) is nonzero, and zero otherwise.

references.title: David Vogan, Review of Harmonic Analysis on Compact Groups, §§2.1–2.16
Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6

items.axiom_audit: AC is used for normalized Haar and Hilbert Riesz; no norm-continuity claim for arbitrary T.
items.proof_strategy: The definition and Riesz argument give linearity and ||A(T)||≤||T||. For h∈K, substitute k↦hk in the weak scalar integral using left invariance to obtain σ(h)A(T)=A(T)π(h); hence every image is an intertwiner. If T intertwines, its integrand equals T for all k, so A(T)=T. Therefore A²=A and the range is Hom_K. If Hom_K contains a nonzero S, then A(S)=S and ||A||≥1 after normalizing S; otherwise A is the zero map. This proves the precise norm statement.

items.title: L² convolution on a compact group is Hilbert–Schmidt
items.statement: Assume AC. For a compact Hausdorff group K with normalized Haar probability μ and f∈L²(K,μ), left convolution C_f on L²(K), (C_fh)(x)=∫K f(xy−1)h(y)dμ(y), is a representative-independent Hilbert–Schmidt operator with ||C_f||HS=||f||₂; in particular it is compact.

references.title: Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6
David Vogan, Review of Harmonic Analysis on Compact Groups, §§2.1–2.16

items.axiom_audit: AC supplies Haar probability and the published arbitrary-Hilbert-basis kernel theorem.
items.proof_strategy: Choose a Borel representative of f and put q(x,y)=f(xy−1). The multiplication/inversion map is continuous, so q is product measurable. Right invariance of normalized Haar gives ∫∫|q(x,y)|²dμ(x)dμ(y)=||f||₂², even for nonmetrizable K. Apply the published L²-kernel theorem, including representative independence and Hilbert–Schmidt norm, then Hilbert–Schmidt compactness. This operator acts on the regular representation only.

items.title: Finite-rank conjugation orbits are operator-norm continuous
items.statement: Assume AC. For a strongly continuous unitary representation π:G→U(H) and a bounded finite-rank T∈B(H), the map g↦π(g)Tπ(g)−1 is continuous in operator norm.

references.title: Vera Serganova, Representation Theory, Chapter III §§1.6–2.1

items.axiom_audit: AC supplies the Countable Choice hypothesis of Hilbert Riesz representation for the coordinate functionals of an arbitrary bounded finite-rank operator.
items.proof_strategy: Choose a finite orthonormal basis a_j of the range of T. Each coordinate functional x↦⟨Tx,a_j⟩ is bounded; the published Hilbert Riesz theorem under Countable Choice supplied by AC gives b_j with ⟨Tx,a_j⟩=⟨x,b_j⟩. Thus T is a finite sum of rank-one maps x↦⟨x,b_j⟩a_j. Unitary conjugation sends each summand to x↦⟨x,π(g)b_j⟩π(g)a_j. The norm difference of rank-one maps is bounded by ||a_j(g)-a_j(h)||||b_j(g)||+||a_j(h)||||b_j(g)-b_j(h)||; strong continuity of the two vector orbits makes each term tend to zero. A finite sum stays norm continuous.

items.title: A positive rank-one Haar average is a nonzero compact intertwiner
items.statement: Assume AC. Let π be a strongly continuous unitary representation of compact Hausdorff K on a nonzero complex Hilbert space H and ξ≠0. With Rξ(x)=⟨x,ξ⟩ξ, the operator Qξ=∫Kπ(k)Rξπ(k)−1dμ(k) is a nonzero positive compact operator commuting with π(K).

references.title: Vera Serganova, Representation Theory, Chapter III §§1.6–2.1
Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6

items.axiom_audit: AC supplies Haar and countable selections for the Bochner approximation and compact-operator norm limit.
items.proof_strategy: The conjugation orbit is norm continuous by the preceding lemma, lies in the rank-one compact operators, and has compact norm image. Under AC choose finite norm nets of that image to make measurable finite-valued simple approximations converging uniformly; Bochner integrability follows on the probability space. Their integrals are finite linear combinations of compact operators, and norm convergence of integrals makes Qξ compact. Left Haar invariance gives π(h)Qξπ(h)−1=Qξ. For every x, ⟨Qξx,x⟩=∫|⟨x,π(k)ξ⟩|²≥0. At x=ξ the integrand is positive at e and on a nonempty open neighborhood, so Haar full support gives ⟨Qξξ,ξ⟩>0.

items.title: A nonzero compact scalar identity forces finite dimension
items.statement: If H is a real or complex Hilbert space and cI_H is compact for c≠0, then H is finite dimensional. This implication is choice free.

references.title: Vera Serganova, Representation Theory, Chapter III §§1.6–2.1

items.axiom_audit: The compact-ball-to-finite-dimension direction of the cited supplier is choice free.
items.proof_strategy: Compose the compact operator cI_H with the bounded scalar operator c−1I_H to obtain compact I_H. Thus the closure of I_H applied to the closed unit ball is the closed unit ball itself and is compact. The published unit-ball criterion then gives a finite ordered basis of H. The zero space is included.

items.title: Irreducible unitary representations of compact groups are finite dimensional
items.statement: Assume AC. Every irreducible strongly continuous unitary representation of a compact Hausdorff group on a nonzero complex Hilbert space is finite dimensional.

references.title: Vera Serganova, Representation Theory, Chapter III §§1.6–2.1
Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6
Bekka, de la Harpe and Valette, Kazhdan's Property (T), Appendix A §A.5

items.axiom_audit: AC is spent in Haar averaging, the compact-operator limit, and the published unitary Schur lemma.
items.proof_strategy: Choose ξ≠0 and form the positive nonzero compact commuting Qξ. Unitary Schur’s lemma, under AC, makes Qξ=cI with c≠0. The compact-scalar lemma forces H finite dimensional. This argument does not assert that integrated convolution in an arbitrary irreducible representation is compact and does not use Peter–Weyl.

items.title: Schur orthogonality for general compact groups
items.statement: Assume AC. If π and ρ are irreducible strongly continuous unitary representations of compact Hausdorff K, their matrix coefficients are orthogonal in L²(K) when π and ρ are inequivalent. For one irreducible π of degree d and vectors v,w,v′,w′, ∫K⟨π(k)v,w⟩ overline{⟨π(k)v′,w′⟩}dμ(k)=d−1⟨v,v′⟩⟨w′,w⟩. Equivalent models obey the same formula after a unitary intertwiner identifies their carriers.

references.title: Vera Serganova, Representation Theory, Chapter III §§1.6–2.1
David Vogan, Review of Harmonic Analysis on Compact Groups, §§2.1–2.16
Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6

items.axiom_audit: AC enters through the Haar, finite-dimensionality and unitary-Schur suppliers.
items.proof_strategy: Finite dimensionality is already proved. For rank-one T:Vρ→Vπ, Tx=⟨x,v′⟩v, average T over K; the weak average is an intertwiner. If π,ρ are inequivalent, Schur makes it zero. If π=ρ, Schur makes it cI and trace invariance gives c=tr(T)/d=⟨v,v′⟩/d. Evaluate ⟨A(T)w′,w⟩ to obtain the displayed integral, retaining first-variable linearity. The d=1 case is included.

items.title: Compact-group isotypic projection
items.statement: Assume AC. For an irreducible strongly continuous unitary σ of compact Hausdorff K of dimension dσ and any strongly continuous unitary π on H, define Pσv=dσ∫K overline{χσ(k)}π(k)v dμ(k), where χσ(k)=tr σ(k) and the integral is vector-valued. No sum over the unitary dual is asserted here. The σ-isotypic subspace means the closed linear span of all invariant subspaces unitarily equivalent to σ.

references.title: Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6
David Vogan, Review of Harmonic Analysis on Compact Groups, §§2.1–2.16

items.axiom_audit: AC supplies Haar probability and the Bochner integral construction.
items.strategy: The finite dimension theorem defines χσ. For fixed v, k↦overline{χσ(k)}π(k)v is norm continuous on compact K and bounded; finite norm nets of its compact image give strongly measurable simple approximations and hence a Bochner integral. Its norm is bounded by dσ∫|χσ(k)|dμ(k)||v||. The next theorem proves that this formula is a projection without assuming Peter–Weyl density.

items.title: Isotypic projections are mutually orthogonal equivariant projections
items.statement: Assume AC. For every irreducible σ of compact Hausdorff K and every strongly continuous unitary π on H, Pσ is a bounded self-adjoint idempotent commuting with π(K), fixes every σ-subrepresentation, and has range equal to the σ-isotypic subspace. If σ and τ are inequivalent, PσPτ=0 and their ranges are orthogonal. No assertion is made that the sum of all Pσ is I_H.

references.title: David Vogan, Review of Harmonic Analysis on Compact Groups, §§2.1–2.16
Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6

items.axiom_audit: AC supplies Haar, Bochner integration and the Schur-orthogonality chain.
items.proof_strategy: The Bochner bound gives boundedness; χσ is central, so Haar conjugation invariance makes Pσ commute with π. Unitarity and k↦k−1 invariance give Pσ*=Pσ. By Schur orthogonality and trace, on any irreducible τ-copy Pσ acts as I for τ≃σ and zero otherwise. To prove its range without Peter–Weyl, fix v and an orthonormal basis e_i of Vσ, and set A_i(w)=∫K⟨w,σ(k)e_i⟩π(k)v dμ(k). Left invariance gives A_iσ(h)=π(h)A_i; its invariant kernel is all of irreducible Vσ or zero, so each image is a finite-dimensional σ-copy or zero. The identity Pσv=dσΣ_i A_i(e_i) puts Pσv in their finite sum. Since Pσ fixes every such copy and is bounded, it fixes their closed span, while every Pσv lies in that span. Thus Pσ²=Pσ and its closed range is exactly the σ-isotypic subspace. For inequivalent τ the range of Pτ consists of τ-copies, killed by Pσ; self-adjointness then gives orthogonal ranges.

title: Complete Reducibility for Compact Groups — Examples

items.title: A circle representation with an averaged orthogonal weight form
items.statement: Assume AC. On V=C² let ρ(z)=diag(1,z) for z∈S¹ and h0(v,w)=2v1 overline{w1}+v1 overline{w2}+v2 overline{w1}+3v2 overline{w2}. The normalized Haar average of h0 is h(v,w)=2v1 overline{w1}+3v2 overline{w2}; the two weight lines become orthogonal.

references.title: Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6
Vera Serganova, Representation Theory, Chapter III §§1.6–2.1

items.axiom_audit: AC supplies the general compact Haar interface; the circle integral itself uses only its given measure.
items.proof_strategy: The unit circle is a closed bounded subset of the real coordinate plane of C and hence compact by Heine–Borel; multiplication and inversion are continuous. The Hermitian matrix [[2,1],[1,3]] is positive definite because its leading minor is 2 and determinant is 5. Substitute ρ(z) into h0: diagonal terms stay 2 and 3, while cross terms acquire z or overline z. Haar invariance under z↦−z gives ∫z=∫overline z=0, leaving diag(2,3). Check that the original off-diagonal form is not invariant and that the averaged form is positive invariant.

items.title: Isotypic Haar projections specialize to finite character sums
items.statement: Assume AC. For a finite group F with discrete topology, a unitary π and irreducible σ of degree dσ, the compact-group formula is Pσ=(dσ/|F|)Σg∈F overline{χσ(g)}π(g). It is the ordinary character idempotent and projects onto the σ-isotypic subspace.

references.title: David Vogan, Review of Harmonic Analysis on Compact Groups, §§2.1–2.16
Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6

items.axiom_audit: AC is inherited from the general isotypic-projection theorem; the finite sum is choice free.
items.proof_strategy: A finite discrete group is compact. Normalized Haar invariance gives the same singleton mass c for every g∈F, and finite additivity gives |F|c=1, so c=1/|F|. Replace the integral in Pσ by the finite sum. The A-page theorem gives idempotence and the image; alternatively Schur orthogonality makes the sum identity on σ and zero on inequivalent irreducibles. The trivial and one-dimensional cases use exactly the same normalization.

items.title: A compact group with no faithful finite-dimensional representation
items.statement: The binary product K=∏n≥0(C₂) with its product topology is a compact Hausdorff group, but every continuous finite-dimensional complex representation of K has a nontrivial kernel. The compactness and no-faithful-representation argument are choice free.

references.title: Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6
David Vogan, Review of Harmonic Analysis on Compact Groups, §§2.1–2.16

items.axiom_audit: Compactness is proved directly by a definable least-child argument on the binary tree; no form of choice or Tychonoff is used.
items.proof_strategy: Identify K with binary-sequence space; finite-coordinate cylinders form a clopen basis and coordinatewise multiplication and inversion are continuous. To prove compactness in ZF, suppose an open cover has no finite subcover. Call a finite binary word bad when its cylinder has no finite subcover; the empty word is bad. At least one of the two children of any bad word is bad, since finite covers of both children combine into a finite cover of the parent. Recursively take the least bad child, choosing 0 when both are bad, to obtain a definite infinite path x all of whose prefix cylinders are bad. An open cover member containing x contains some prefix cylinder, a contradiction. Distinct paths are separated by clopen cylinders, so K is Hausdorff. For a continuous ρ:K→GL(V), finite-dimensional coordinate norm equivalence makes ρ operator-norm continuous at e. Choose a product cylinder subgroup N fixing finitely many initial coordinates with ||ρ(g)−I||<1 for every g∈N. Every g∈N has order two. If ρ(g)≠I, choose v with w=(ρ(g)−I)v≠0; then ρ(g)w=−w and ||ρ(g)−I||≥2, contradiction. Thus N⊆kerρ and contains a nonidentity tail element, so ρ is not faithful.

items.title: No normalized translation-invariant Haar measure on the real line
items.statement: For the noncompact additive group R, every nonzero left Haar measure has infinite total mass; therefore the compact-group normalized Haar averaging construction has no finite invariant Haar probability on R. This implication is choice free conditional on a given Haar measure.

references.title: Bekka, de la Harpe and Valette, Kazhdan's Property (T), Appendix A §A.5
Emmanuel Kowalski, An Introduction to the Representation Theory of Groups, §§5.2–5.6

items.axiom_audit: No choice is used once a nonzero Haar measure is given; the example does not claim Haar nonexistence.
items.proof_strategy: Let μ be any nonzero left Haar measure on R. The open interval (0,1) has c=μ((0,1))>0 by Haar full support. Its translates (2n,2n+1), n≥0, are pairwise disjoint and each has mass c by translation invariance. Countable additivity gives μ(R)≥Σn≥0c=∞. Thus no scalar rescaling makes μ(R)=1; compactness is exactly what allowed normalized finite averaging.
